content: Juniperus communis (juniper) has specific dosing recommendations based on its intended use. For oral administration, follow the manufacturer's instructions, such as 800 mg taken twice daily (PO BID). Alternatively, 1-2 grams of juniper berries can be taken orally three times daily (PO TID). Another method involves consuming one cup of tea made by steeping 1 teaspoon of crushed berries (2-3 grams) in 150 mL of boiling water for 10 minutes, taken three times daily. A liquid preparation of 2 mL can also be taken orally three times daily. Juniper is used for various conditions, including dyspepsia, flatulence, heartburn, bloating, loss of appetite, urinary tract infections (UTIs), kidney and bladder stones, snake bites, intestinal worms, gastrointestinal infections, diabetes, and cancer. When applied topically, it may help alleviate rheumatic pains, inflammatory diseases, and wounds. However, there is insufficient reliable information to confirm its effectiveness for these uses. Juniper is known to have diuretic properties, but excessive doses may cause kidney damage. Juniper may interact with diuretic medications, such as amiloride, bendroflumethiazide, bumetanide, chlorothiazide, chlorthalidone, cyclopenthiazide, drospirenone, ethacrynic acid, furosemide, hydrochlorothiazide, indapamide, methyclothiazide, metolazone, spironolactone, torsemide, and triamterene. It can either potentiate or interfere with the effects of these diuretics. Due to its diuretic properties, caution and close monitoring are advised when using juniper alongside these medications, as high doses may lead to kidney damage. Juniper may also interact with antidiabetic medications, including acarbose, glimepiride, glipizide, glyburide, insulin (aspart, detemir, glargine, glulisine, lispro, NPH, and regular human insulin), metformin, miglitol, nateglinide, pioglitazone, repaglinide, rosiglitazone, saxagliptin, sitagliptin, and vildagliptin. These interactions are thought to occur through pharmacodynamic synergism, theoretically increasing the risk of hypoglycemia. While the significance of these interactions is unknown, close monitoring is recommended. Regarding pregnancy, juniper should be avoided as it may cause uterine contractions and kidney inflammation. It is categorized as unsafe for use during pregnancy. Information on its safety during lactation is not available. Controlled studies in pregnant women have not shown evidence of fetal risk, but caution is still advised.
